k~nT[w@I74?hEM,mV=cc.text:
Welcome to Neo-GSE!
Okay, lemme tell ya the basics:
Speed is basically Sonic's X Velocity on-ground. Changing X Velocity or Y Velocity accomplishes nothing if Midair = 0.
If Midair = Y, changing those variables will do something however. Speed is the useless variable in the realm of air.
Also, keep in mind that changing any X or Y related variable will have the opposite effect of normal Scratch movement. This has to do with how tomicool coded the scrolling. Essentially, changing Y Scroll by 10 will move the player downward, not upward.
Also, if you plan on making Sonic jump or detatch from the ground in a special way during a move, you'll want the minimalistic jump code. I'll put that right below this comment. :)
One concept you'll need to wrap your mind around for GSE is that there's a "Display Sprite" and a "Collision Sprite" for... darn well everything. The Display Sprites will handle what the user sees, while the Collision Sprites handle the underlying gameplay, such as character movement. One way to easily see what is what is to check for a block like "Set ghost effect to (100)". This makes the sprite hide while its collision elements can still be detected by other Collision Sprites. This is Sonic's Collision Sprite, so it handles everything Sonic touches and his related physics.

Fec_3(*2):MmQrd7B)US.text:
Welcome to the Stage Collision sprite! I guess I may as well mention it here, but see that little block that sets the "Scratch Version" variable? Well, in case you are aware of what this does, congrats. Set it to "S2" if you're using 2.0, and "S3" if you're using 3.0. Also, if you're designing an entirely new level, you should probably change 115% to 100%.
If you don't know... WELL IT'S STORY TIIIIME
So back in the day of Scratch 2, all vectors were nice and clean and they never looked pixellated or bitmap-y. Most of us would in fact say this was the POINT of bitmap, and argued that vector was a better and cooler way to do animations and stages than basically anything else. However, when Scratch 3 was originally teased, we saw a vector that genuinely looked worse than bitmap. instead of being clean and rounded, it looked a bit blurry and pixellated. This was especially true if you were using it to create vast stages. You can try setting the variable to "S2" if you're in 3.0, and you can see the effect it has on the stage and its appearance. It's better than it first was, but it's still not good.
HOWEVER, before Scratch 3 was even properly released, I came up with a solution and it still works to this day. If you scale up your entire Scratch 2 stage (in the Scratch 2 costume editor) to nine times its original size, and then set the size to 100%, you can get a much cleaner-looking level in Scratch 3. This breaks the Scratch 2 version and isn't exactly ideal, but it works and can help you make your levels look 9x as nice.
There's a full tutorial here if you're still not getting it:
https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/272689985/

I might patch this out later, but until then if you're making a new level for the Scratch 3 fix, just use my tutorial and make sure you set the size to 100 in both of these stage sprites!

Y*;OE7m4pkwd8n.;zhSf.text:
Here's the animation code for the Spindash's new look!
Currently, it's frame-locked, so you can't just insert new frames into the animation on a whim. I should probably change that sometime, but I'll break it down anyway!
Firstly, the two major players in this animation are "P1 Anim-Frame" and "Alternate".
"P1 Anim-Frame" is just the frame of the Spindash animation being used. "Spin Dash 1" will be used if we set the variable to 1, "Spin Dash 2" will be used if we set the variable to 2, etc.
We have six different frames of Spin Dash animation-- the first five have this sort of revving look to them, and the sixth is more of a neutral position with also different proportions. I decided the pattern should be: 1, 6, 2, 6, 3, 6, 4, 6, 5, 6... as that creates a nice shaking animation along with the revving one. 
That's where "Alternate" comes in. It counts up from 0 to 11-- twelve frames-- and resets back to 0 after 11. When the number is even, P1 Anim-Frame gets set to 6. When the number is odd, P1 Anim-Frame is set to a value between 1 and 6. That means that after the revving there's always three frames of time spent on the sixth frame of the animation.

``H*_3KYu:_H~58;G?q;.text: This is a simple check for whether the value of Alternate is even or odd.
